lesson.title: Know what a number means

lead.text: Start with the file. When a program reads a line such as 11 biscuits, the 11 arrives with quotation marks around it, as text. Python calls every kind of value a type, and it has a separate type for each job. Text is a str, short for string. A whole number is an int, short for integer. The number 12 is an int, and '12' in quotation marks is a str that happens to contain the characters 1 and 2.

The difference matters because one symbol does different jobs for different types. Between two ints, + adds, so 3 + 4 gives 7. Between two strs, + joins them end to end, so '3' + '4' gives '34'. The picture runs both versions with the values '12' and '3'.

afterFigure.text: To get arithmetic out of text, convert it first. int('12') reads the characters and returns the whole number 12, and that happens before + sees the values. Quotation marks make text even when the characters are digits, so a program has to say when it wants a number.

lead.text: Both values below start as text. int() turns each one into a whole number before the + gets to work.

Now the bakery. With both values converted, the program has 11 biscuits and 4 plates. Sharing them out is division, and Python has three division operators because there are three questions you might ask. The answer to a division is called the quotient.

The first operator, /, divides exactly and gives a decimal answer, so 11 / 4 is 2.75. A number with a decimal part is a float. The second, //, is floor division, and it gives the number of whole groups: 11 // 4 is 2, so each plate gets 2 biscuits. The third, %, gives the remainder, the amount left once the whole groups have been taken out. 11 % 4 is 3.

Between them, // and % split a quantity into whole groups and a leftover, which is how the bakery can say two each with three left over. Multiply back to check: 2 × 4 + 3 is 11. One more operator is worth knowing. ** raises a number to a power, so 2 ** 3 means 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8.
The bakery has 11 biscuits and 4 plates. Use what you know about whole groups and leftovers.

So far every number was positive. Negative numbers show what // really does. Floor division rounds down, to the whole number on the left of the exact answer on a number line. For positive numbers that looks like dropping the decimal part: 7 // 2 is 3, because 3.5 rounds down to 3. With a negative answer the two ideas part company. The exact answer to −7 / 2 is −3.5, and the whole number just below −3.5 is −4, so −7 // 2 is −4.
The picture runs the biscuit sum twice. In the first case a is 11 and b is 4, as before. In the second case a is −11.

afterFigure.text: In the second case the exact answer is −2.75, and rounding down gives −3, not −2. The remainder follows from the quotient. It is what is left after the whole groups are taken back out, so −11 − (−3 × 4) = −11 + 12 = 1. When the number you divide by is positive, the remainder is never negative, even if the number being divided is.

The remainder is what the whole groups leave behind.

lead.text: Back to / for a moment. Its answers are floats, and floats have a limit you should know about before trusting them with money. A computer stores a float using only 0s and 1s, and in that system some decimals have no exact form, just as one third has no exact decimal form: 0.333 and so on without end. The decimal 0.1 is one of the awkward ones. Python keeps the nearest value it can, which is very slightly off.

Usually the error is far too small to see. It shows when you compare. The symbol == asks whether two values are equal and answers True or False, a value of type bool. The sum 0.1 * 3 comes out as 0.30000000000000004, so 0.1 * 3 == 0.3 is False even though the two sides agree on paper. That is why money is often held in whole pence, and why exact comparisons of floats are avoided.
Whole numbers have no such problem. An int is stored exactly, and it can grow as large as the computer's memory allows.
Work out whether the two sides of the comparison hold exactly the same stored value.

Comparisons give True or False, and Python can read any other value as a yes or no in the same way. The function bool() shows how it reads a value. Zero gives False. The value False gives False. Empty text, written '' with nothing between the quotation marks, gives False. Every other value gives True.

That rule catches people out with data from files, where everything arrives as text. The string 'False' has characters in it, so bool('False') is True. So is bool('0'). All Python checks is whether any characters are there, and what they spell makes no difference. To test for the word False, compare the text with 'False' or convert it first.
A blank field in a file arrives as empty text, so bool() is a quick way to spot a missing entry.
Four values go through bool(). Decide for each whether Python reads it as yes or no, then count the yeses.

lesson.orientation: Separate numeric values from text and choose arithmetic deliberately.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A bakery keeps its orders in a file, and one line reads 11 biscuits, 4 plates. Someone wants to know how many biscuits each plate gets and how many are left in the box. You can do that in your head: two each, with three left over. Getting Python to say it takes a little more care.

Python needs to know what kind of thing each value is before it will do anything with it. A file hands over everything as text, so the 11 and the 4 arrive looking like numbers without being numbers. Add them as they stand and they stick together instead of giving 15.

This lesson follows those two values from the file to an answer. First comes telling text from numbers and converting one into the other. Next the biscuits are shared out, which takes three kinds of division and raises a question about negative numbers. The last two stops are places where numbers surprise people: decimals that are slightly off, and what Python counts as true.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell text from numbers in Python, and use / and // and % to split a quantity exactly.

recap.keyIdea: A value's type decides what an operator does. Convert text before doing sums, and use // and % to split a quantity into whole groups and a leftover.

blocks.text: Back at the bakery, you shared 11 biscuits as 2 each with 3 left over. Along the way you found that −13 // 5 is −3, that a sum of decimals can miss its target by a hair, and that two of the four values you tested count as True.

recap.nextHook: A piece of text is a row of characters, and the next lesson cuts out exactly the characters you want, using positions that start at zero like the marks on a ruler.

questions.prompt: How many of these are True: bool(0), bool('0'), bool(''), bool('False')?

'0' and 'False' are strings. Do they have characters?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: bool('0') and bool('False') are True. bool(0) and bool('') are False.

questions.onCorrect: 2. '0' and 'False' are non-empty strings, so both are True. 0 and '' give False.

misconceptions.feedback: Check 'False' and '0' again. They are strings with characters in them, not the number 0.
bool(0) is False, because zero counts as empty.
Non-empty strings count as True whatever they spell.
